title: BMI Calculation Methodology
overview: Body Mass Index (BMI) is a simple calculation using height and weight to estimate body fat. While widely used for population-level health screening, it has limitations for individual assessment.

methods.name: Standard BMI (Quetelet Index)
methods.description: The original BMI formula developed by Belgian mathematician Adolphe Quetelet between 1830-1850. It divides weight in kilograms by height in meters squared.
limitations: Does not distinguish between muscle and fat mass
May overestimate body fat in athletes
May underestimate body fat in elderly
Does not account for fat distribution
methods.author: Adolphe Quetelet

methods.name: New BMI (Trefethen)
methods.description: A revised formula proposed by Oxford mathematician Nick Trefethen in 2013 that better accounts for the relationship between height and weight across different heights.
limitations: Same fundamental limitations as standard BMI
methods.bestFor: Very tall or very short individuals
methods.author: Nick Trefethen

methods.name: Asian-Adjusted BMI
methods.description: WHO recommends lower BMI thresholds for Asian populations due to higher health risks at lower BMI levels. Overweight starts at 23 kg/m² instead of 25 kg/m².
methods.accuracy: Better risk prediction for Asian populations
limitations: May not apply uniformly to all Asian ethnicities

sources.name: Quetelet, A. - Sur l'homme et le développement de ses facultés
WHO Expert Consultation - Asian BMI cutoffs

footnotes: BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnostic measure
Consult a healthcare provider for comprehensive health assessment
Athletes and muscular individuals may have high BMI with low body fat
disclaimer: BMI is intended for screening purposes only. It does not diagnose body fatness or health status. Consult a healthcare professional for medical advice.
